Latent Class and Rank Analysis

Source: vignettes/latent-class-rank.Rmd
latent-class-rank.Rmd

Note: Some computationally intensive examples below are shown with eval=FALSE to keep CRAN build times short. For full rendered output, see the pkgdown site.

library(exametrika)

Latent Class Analysis (LCA)

LCA classifies examinees into unordered latent classes. Specify the dataset and the number of classes.

LCA(J15S500, ncls = 5)

The Class Membership Matrix indicates which latent class each examinee belongs to:

result.LCA <- LCA(J15S500, ncls = 5)
head(result.LCA$Students)

LCA Plot Types

  • IRP: Item Reference Profile
  • CMP: Class Membership Profile
  • TRP: Test Reference Profile
  • LCD: Latent Class Distribution
plot(result.LCA, type = "IRP", items = 1:6, nc = 2, nr = 3)

plot(result.LCA, type = "CMP", students = 1:9, nc = 3, nr = 3)

plot(result.LCA, type = "TRP")

plot(result.LCA, type = "LCD")

Latent Rank Analysis (LRA)

LRA is similar to LCA but assumes an ordering among the latent classes (ranks). Specify the dataset and the number of ranks.

Rank membership probabilities and rank-up/rank-down odds are calculated:

result.LRA <- LRA(J15S500, nrank = 6)
head(result.LRA$Students)

plot(result.LRA, type = "IRP", items = 1:6, nc = 2, nr = 3)

plot(result.LRA, type = "RMP", students = 1:9, nc = 3, nr = 3)

plot(result.LRA, type = "TRP")

plot(result.LRA, type = "LRD")

Classifying New Respondents with predict()

Once a model is fitted, predict() assigns new respondents to its classes or ranks. The estimated parameters are held fixed and one E-step is run on the new responses, so the new respondents do not change the model. This is useful when the model is built on one group and applied to another, for example a later cohort that took the same test.

Here the model is fitted to the first 400 examinees and then used to classify the remaining 100.

X <- J15S500$U
X[J15S500$Z == 0] <- NA
fit <- LRA(dataFormat(X[1:400, ]), nrank = 6)
pred <- predict(fit, X[401:500, ])
pred
#> Prediction from a LRA fit: 100 respondents, 6 ranks
#> 
#> Latent rank distribution of the estimates:
#> Rank1 Rank2 Rank3 Rank4 Rank5 Rank6 
#>    13    20    17    19    16    15
head(round(pred$Membership, 3))
#>          Rank1 Rank2 Rank3 Rank4 Rank5 Rank6
#> Student1 0.000 0.003 0.048 0.057 0.163 0.729
#> Student2 0.323 0.410 0.138 0.128 0.001 0.000
#> Student3 0.006 0.150 0.312 0.216 0.127 0.189
#> Student4 0.000 0.007 0.098 0.573 0.275 0.047
#> Student5 0.071 0.090 0.627 0.155 0.058 0.000
#> Student6 0.012 0.116 0.417 0.288 0.159 0.008
head(pred$Estimate)
#> Student1 Student2 Student3 Student4 Student5 Student6 
#>        6        2        3        4        3        3

newdata can be a matrix or data frame with the items in columns, or an object made by dataFormat(). Items are matched by name, so the columns may come in any order and extra columns are ignored; a missing item is an error. Missing responses (NA, or the codes given in na) are simply left out of the likelihood, so a respondent who answered only some items still gets a membership. Polytomous responses must use the coding of the fitted data; a category that the fitted data never used for an item cannot be scored and is treated as missing, with a warning.

pred$log_lik holds each respondent’s log-likelihood under the model. Summed over held-out respondents, it gives a predictive criterion for comparing models fitted to the same training data:

fit4 <- LRA(dataFormat(X[1:400, ]), nrank = 4)
c(
  nrank4 = sum(predict(fit4, X[401:500, ])$log_lik),
  nrank6 = sum(pred$log_lik)
)
#>    nrank4    nrank6 
#> -831.3531 -832.0329

On the data a model was fitted to, predict() reproduces the memberships stored in the fit. It works the same way for LCA() and for Biclustering() / Ranklustering, with binary, nominal, ordinal and rated data; for biclustering the field memberships of the items are held fixed as well.

LRA for Ordinal Data

LRA can also handle ordinal scale data. The mic option enforces monotonic increasing constraints.

result.LRAord <- LRA(J15S3810, nrank = 3, mic = TRUE)

Score-rank relationship visualizations:

plot(result.LRAord, type = "ScoreFreq")
plot(result.LRAord, type = "ScoreRank")

Item-rank relationship plots:

  • ICBR: Item Category Boundary Reference – cumulative probability curves for each category threshold
  • ICRP: Item Category Response Profile – probability of each response category across ranks
plot(result.LRAord, type = "ICBR", items = 1:4, nc = 2, nr = 2)
plot(result.LRAord, type = "ICRP", items = 1:4, nc = 2, nr = 2)

Rank membership profiles for individual examinees:

plot(result.LRAord, type = "RMP", students = 1:9, nc = 3, nr = 3)

LRA for Rated/Nominal Data

For multiple-choice tests (nominal scale), LRA can analyze response patterns including distractor choices.

result.LRArated <- LRA(J35S5000, nrank = 10, mic = TRUE)
plot(result.LRArated, type = "ScoreFreq")
plot(result.LRArated, type = "ScoreRank")
plot(result.LRArated, type = "ICRP", items = 1:4, nc = 2, nr = 2)

Reference

Shojima, K. (2022). Test Data Engineering. Springer.
